title: Failure of Unique Factorization in Z[sqrt(-5)]
description: The classic counterexample showing Z[sqrt(-5)] is not a UFD: 6 = 2*3 = (1+sqrt(-5))(1-sqrt(-5)) gives two distinct irreducible factorizations.

meta.author: Kummer, Dedekind (formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib)

mathlibDependencies.description: Element is irreducible in a monoid

openQuestion: Can the failure of unique factorization in Z[sqrt(-5)] be formalized as a counterexample showing it is not a UFD?
significance: This is the classical counterexample that motivated Kummer's ideal numbers (1847) and Dedekind's theory of ideals (1871). Z[sqrt(-5)] has class number 2, meaning the failure of unique factorization is measured by the class group Z/2Z. The formalization proves all four factors (2, 3, 1+sqrt(-5), 1-sqrt(-5)) are irreducible, that they give two genuinely different factorizations of 6, and that this implies Z[sqrt(-5)] is not a UFD via the irreducible-but-not-prime argument.

overview.historicalContext: The failure of unique factorization in rings of algebraic integers was one of the great crises of 19th-century number theory. Ernst Kummer discovered in the 1840s that his attempted proof of Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes broke down because unique factorization fails in cyclotomic rings $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. To rescue his approach, Kummer invented 'ideal numbers' (1847), which Richard Dedekind later refined into the modern theory of ideals (1871). The ring $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is the simplest and most famous counterexample: it has class number 2, meaning its ideal class group is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, and the failure of unique factorization is precisely measured by this non-trivial class group. The factorization $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ appears in virtually every algebraic number theory textbook as the motivating example for the entire theory of Dedekind domains.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize the classical counterexample: $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})$ gives two essentially different irreducible factorizations in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, proving this ring is not a UFD.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof uses the norm function $N(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$, which is multiplicative and non-negative. The strategy has three phases: (1) compute the norms of all factors and verify the two factorizations; (2) prove all four factors are irreducible by showing that a norm factorization $N(z) = N(a) \cdot N(b)$ forces one factor to be a unit, exploiting the gaps in the norm image (no elements of norm 2 or 3); (3) prove the factorizations are essentially different by showing $2 \nmid (1 + \sqrt{-5})$, which means 2 is irreducible but not prime — the hallmark of non-UFD behavior.
keyInsights: The norm $N(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$ reduces irreducibility in an algebraic number ring to Diophantine equations over $\mathbb{Z}$ — a powerful technique used throughout algebraic number theory
The gap in the norm image (no elements of norm 2 or 3, since $a^2 + 5b^2 \in \{2,3\}$ has no integer solutions) is what forces irreducibility of elements with small norm

The distinction between 'irreducible' and 'prime' is the precise obstruction to unique factorization: in a UFD these coincide, and in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ they diverge because $2 \mid (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ but $2 \nmid (1 \pm \sqrt{-5})$

The class number $h = 2$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ means unique factorization 'almost' holds — it fails by the minimal possible amount, with the ideal class group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ measuring the failure

This counterexample motivated the entire edifice of algebraic number theory: Kummer's ideal numbers, Dedekind's ideals, and the modern theory of Dedekind domains where unique factorization of elements is replaced by unique factorization of ideals

sections.title: The Ring Z[sqrt(-5)] and Its Norm
sections.summary: Defines the norm N(a + b*sqrt(-5)) = a^2 + 5b^2 and proves its multiplicativity and unit characterization (units have norm 1).

sections.title: The Two Factorizations of 6
sections.summary: Exhibits and verifies the two factorizations: 6 = 2*3 = (1+sqrt(-5))*(1-sqrt(-5)).

sections.title: Norms of the Factors
sections.summary: Computes N(2) = 4, N(3) = 9, N(1 +/- sqrt(-5)) = 6, N(6) = 36, confirming norm multiplicativity.

sections.title: Irreducibility of the Factors
sections.summary: Proves all four factors are non-units and irreducible. The key lemma: no element has norm 2 or 3, so norm factorization forces one factor to be a unit.

sections.title: The Factorizations Are Essentially Different
sections.summary: Proves 2 does not divide (1+sqrt(-5)), establishing that 2 is irreducible but not prime, which proves Z[sqrt(-5)] is not a UFD.

conclusion.summary: This formalization provides a complete, axiom-free, sorry-free proof that $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a unique factorization domain. It exhibits two essentially different irreducible factorizations of 6 and proves their distinctness by showing 2 is irreducible but not prime. The proof is entirely constructive, using only the multiplicative norm and elementary Diophantine arguments.
conclusion.implications: The failure of unique factorization in quadratic integer rings motivated the development of ideal theory and the modern framework of Dedekind domains. In $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, while element factorization is non-unique, ideal factorization is unique: $(6) = (2, 1+\sqrt{-5})^2 \cdot (3, 1+\sqrt{-5})(3, 1-\sqrt{-5})$. This recovery of uniqueness at the level of ideals is the central insight of algebraic number theory.
openQuestions: Can the non-UFD proof be extended to show Z[sqrt(-5)] is a Dedekind domain with unique ideal factorization, using Mathlib's Dedekind domain API?
Can the class number computation h(Z[sqrt(-5)]) = 2 be formalized in Lean, establishing that Z/2Z measures the failure of unique factorization?
Which imaginary quadratic fields Q(sqrt(-d)) have class number 1 (hence are UFDs)? The Baker-Heegner-Stark theorem gives exactly 9 values of d.
